job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the train out of Madrid to the factory of an elevator maker, where I'm a junior embedded engineer. I write the small programs that run inside the door controllers and the safety circuits, test them on a bench, and fix what the testers send back. I studied computer engineering at the Polytechnic and wrote my final project on a sensor for lift doors.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the bench, where a program becomes a door that opens and closes. What wears me out is the strict certification paperwork, because a lift can't fail. I live in a shared flat with two colleagues, I sing in the choir at my church on Sundays, and my girlfriend, Lucía, and I are saving for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, we've heard big promises before. At work I'd carry on as I am and tell my friends to focus on honest work. A lift that fails isn't a software bug, it's somebody's grandmother stuck between floors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. Embedded safety software is slow and strictly checked, and my company's orders are steady because Spain keeps building and renovating. I have no debt and about seven months saved, and my parents would help if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish my probation, take the certification course and learn the safety standards. I'd put 500 euros a month aside for the flat with Lucía. I'd keep going to choir and be at my mother's table on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like an ordinary good year, which I'm grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you and Lucía are saving for a flat. What's the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucía and I want to marry in about three years, so we're saving for a deposit in a town outside Madrid. She works as a nurse, and her shifts help the budget. We've agreed that I'd take the steady job and she'd decide about the extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to explain an error message, or to write a first test. I never use it for anything that goes into a safety function. That has to be written and reviewed by people, as the standard says.

Put **500 euros** a month aside for a flat with Lucía.
Keep going to **choir** and my mother's table on Sundays.
feel: **Calm**, like an ordinary good year that I'm grateful for.

fieldNote: He keeps AI **out of safety functions**, citing the standard.

steps.text: Finish probation and take the lift safety certification course
Put 500 euros a month aside toward a flat deposit
Plan the wedding and the flat with Lucía for three years ahead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change the desk work, and I'd tell colleagues to learn it and stay honest. At work I'd back training days. The companies that tell their people early what's changing will keep their best engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a bit uneasy. Writing test code and documents is already half done by tools, and a team of eight might become six over a few years. The safety-critical code and the bench work stay with us, since certification requires named humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly, since they'll be everywhere, and use them for tests and documentation. I'd also take a course in functional safety, which is a skill few people have. I'd save 600 euros a month and not take any risks with the flat fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I trust that a plan exists. I'm not shaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in your work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Test scripts, documentation and the first draft of simple code. I use it for these about once a week now, and I expect that to become daily. I'd check each one, as I do already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger engineers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the safety standards and the hardware, because that's what keeps their name on the paper. Also to ask their elders for advice. Old engineers who know why a rule exists are worth a lot.

Take a course in **functional safety**, a skill few people have.
Save **600 euros** a month and keep the flat fund safe.

His shelter is functional safety, a regulated niche.

steps.text: Use the AI tools weekly for test scripts and documents
Take a functional safety course after work
Save 600 euros a month for the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and no one should pretend otherwise. At work I'd say we should hold on to humans where safety is involved. Two years isn't enough for a family to change course, and anyone who says it is has never raised a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious. The thinking side of my job, writing code, tests and documents, could be done by a machine in two years, and the company might need half the engineers. Robots for hands-on work come three years later, so the bench and the factory would last a bit longer, but I'm on the software side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 1,000 euros a month, postpone the flat purchase but keep the wedding, because that matters more. I'd ask my parents if we can live with them for the first year. I'd also train as a lift installation technician, because that's hands-on and safety-critical, and my company needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray more, and I'd talk to Lucía every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do about the flat and the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Lucía first, because her nursing job is more secure and hands-on. We'd decide to marry on the date we planned, with a smaller party. A flat can wait, but I wouldn't wait on the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it happened that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the engineers who built it, and not even the companies, really. I'd blame governments that stand by and say nothing, and the people who sell it without caring who gets hurt. And I'd blame myself if I did nothing.

I'd say two years isn't enough for a family to change **course**.

steps.text: Postpone the flat and keep the wedding with a smaller party

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be careful, and I'd tell my friends to start planning. At work I'd suggest every engineer takes a safety or hardware course. Five years is enough to learn a second trade, if you start before the letters arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious but I think I'd cope. Software work would be mostly automated by 2031, but there'd be a place for people who understand the machines and can be held responsible for safety. By then I'd be 27, married and perhaps with a child, so the pressure would be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and finish the safety course in the first year. In the second I'd move to the validation team, where people sign off on the machines. I'd save 700 euros a month and keep the flat plan going, with a smaller flat in a cheaper town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and also grateful for the time. I'd feel that I have a chance to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years would let me move to the bench, the factory floor and the installation side, where robots arrive later. I'd also use the AI tools more, to be good at the thinking part while it lasts. That seems sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your church community do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look after each other, as we always do. Our priest runs a small fund for families in trouble and I'd add to it. Not everyone has savings the way I do, and I'd feel it was my duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and people who work hard and stay humble will be fine. At work I'd keep learning and teach what I know. In ten years a person can build a career, a family and a savings pot, and still learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm. By 32 I'd be an experienced safety engineer and maybe a team lead, married with a child. Robots will come for hands-on work around 2039, but I'd be in a field where law needs a named person. My worry would be the world my child grows up in, more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, finish the flat purchase and have a child. I'd use AI tools more each year, because that's what the next generation will expect. I'd keep going to church and volunteer with the youth choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a gentle worry for the children. A decade lets me breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if the date was 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Present, mostly. I'd want to be home for dinner, not a man who's always at the office. If the machines let us all work less, I'd like to think that's a good thing, as long as people still have dignity and something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of father do you want to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I wouldn't rush the flat, and I'd save more slowly. I'd wait and see how the tools develop before choosing a second trade. It's good to have time to watch.

I'd keep learning and **teach** what I know.
think: I'm fairly **calm**; by 32 I'd be an experienced safety engineer.
My worry would be the **world** my child grows up in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I can plan a wedding and a flat, but I can't plan around a change that arrives in two years. What would help is companies telling staff early, paid training in safety and hardware work, and a community that looks after those who lose out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against these tools. I use them. I just think people should be treated as people, and that work gives dignity as well as money.

headlineQuote: I can plan a wedding and a flat, but I can't plan around a change that arrives in two years.
portrait: Pedro is **22**, a computer engineering graduate working as a junior embedded engineer at an elevator maker near Madrid.
He has no debt, about seven months saved, and is saving with his girlfriend Lucía for a **flat** and wedding.
He is traditional, values work, faith and family, and **blames** governments that stay silent and firms that sell without care.
He is steady: he uses AI tools now and then, moves once change is proven and leans on **safety** certification.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because two years cannot be planned around for a family.
whatWouldHelp: Early **notice** from companies, paid training in safety and hardware work, and community support for those who lose out.
